utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to you, Mr. Dodig.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And before we continue, I would like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave yesterday at the beginning of your testimony. That is, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Carrier, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Dodig.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes Mr. President. There -- I think there was a slight problem with the exhibit list this morning, so if we could just confirm with my friends that they have received it now. I think that some of them may not have been released yet. I just want to make sure that everyone's on the same page. There is also one document, and I have informed my friends that we're still waiting -- the translation is done. It's just a slight holdup in getting it put on the list. So I won't deal with that until after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Unless there's anything in response to be said but -- nothing. Then please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you state that from October 1993 until June 1994, you were the Assistant Minister of Defence. You didn't mention it in your statement but your job during that time was as Assistant Minister, head of Security and Information Service, or SIS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you say is correct, but my curriculum vitae written here was not written by me. It was derived from the documents available to the Defence. If I had known I was supposed to write my own CV, I would have done so. It's correct that I was in the Ministry of Defence, Assistant Minister for Security ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, perhaps -- Mr. Dodig, perhaps already at the beginning we are not unlimited in time. The question was answered by your first sentence. To defend yourself on whether it would have been in your curriculum if it would have been created in a different way is not something that Mr. Carrier has shown to be interested in very much at this moment. So could you please focus your answer on what is asked and apparently, in the question, Mr. Carrier was seeking to know exactly what your duties as an Assistant Minister of Defence were. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And Mr. Dodig, just to follow up on that, because I'm the first person to cross-examine you here, your statements are in evidence so you don't need to repeat those things unless you find it necessary but just to focus in on the questions that I'm asking. Is it fair to say that, even before this trial started and before any of the evidence was called in this case, that you had publicly expressed negative opinions about this Tribunal. For instance, statements to the effect that this Tribunal's indictments, including the one in this case, are politically motivated?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am a public figure, and oftentimes, in the context of my public activity, I express certain opinions on certain developments, and it must have been in that context then. I did not speak about the work of the Tribunal but of its motives, the way I see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have document number 65 ter 7428 up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, what is going to appear on the screen in front of you is an article that appeared in the newspaper Slobodna Dalmacija on the 30th of January, 2001. Sorry, Mr. Dodig, I will get back to you in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that apparently they haven't been released, which is what I was canvassing in the beginning. But apparently that's our fault. I apologise for that. Mr. President, I'm informed by our Case Manager that he is still trying to release the document, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you move then to another subject for the time being, until this is released.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, I apologise to change the train of thought on you. Mr. Dodig, you say in your statement that you heard about Operation Storm at the same time as all the other citizens in Croatia. And I take it by that, that you mean that you learned about the operation when it started on the 4th of August, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dodig, is it fair to say, then, that you were not specifically consulted, nor was your input solicited by anyone from the office of the president, the Main Staff, the Ministry of Defence --

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: -- or the Ministry of Interior in relation to the planning or execution of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody either contacted me nor informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dodig, in the final paragraph of your statement, you explain your understanding of the Prosecution's allegations in this case, that there was a policy to encourage or condone the crimes and discriminations perpetrated against Serbs in the aftermath of Operation Storm, and that was done in order to create a climate of fear, to drive Serbs away from the area. And in that paragraph, you state in effect that these allegations are false. You also state that you probably would have been informed at the time had an allegation of that nature been true. My question is, Mr. Dodig, given that you were not even consulted on the operation itself, why would you think that you would probably have been informed about a related criminal plot against the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me just a moment to see ... Yes, in that last sentence, I wrote that the political position of the government of Croatia -- if the political position of the government of Croatia had been such, I would have been informed. I meant that I would have known during the war if such a tendency had existed. I didn't mean that I would have been informed at one single moment. But I am aware of what the political positions were, the general attitude towards the Serbs in Croatia and their leadership. I have never heard from anyone, not even a hint from the high officials that they had such an attitude towards the Serbian community in Croatia that would support the theory that the became was to expel them from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dodig, following up on that, you mentioned that you had had many meetings and discussions with Mr. Pasic, who was the Croatian government's civil authority representative for Knin. You also state that in your opinion he was exposed to psychological and political terror at the hands of Serbs, apparently those who didn't want or accept any cooperation with Croats and had declared him a traitor for even talking to Croats. Would you then -- in your statement you contrast that with your evaluation of Mr. Pasic's very proper relations with Croats, and you note that he was accepted by all authorities and the Croats in the area. Is that a fair summary of your position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. The community where it happened is a relatively small community, so I know quite a few people, quite a few Croats from the town where Mr. Pasic lived, and they had a very good opinion of him from that time and later. There is not a personal qualification or attitude. It's just my experience of Mr. Pasic as a man who found himself in a very delicate situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: When you say that he was accepted by all authorities, are you talking about all the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the part of the authorities that I was able to relate to at that time. I could not talk to anyone from the top echelon of this Croatian authorities about Mr. Pasic, but I did talk to town mayors, municipal officials, and they all said that Mr. Pasic was a very good, decent man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So despite what you said about knowing how the upper echelon thought in other circumstances, at least in this circumstance, you say you don't really know what their attitude was towards Mr. Pasic, the top echelon?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we please have Exhibit P463 up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, this is a transcript that's coming up on the screen in front of you. And it's from a meeting that was held on the 22nd of August, 1995, between President Tudjman and Dr. Jure Radic at the presidential palace. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could turn to page 5 in the English and page 7 in the B/C/S. And if you could go down to the bottom of the page, please, in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, I'm just going read a bit of an exchange here. This is President Tudjman speaking. He says: "Wait a second, hadn't I sent Cermak to Knin, it would have been horrible there." Dr. Radic replies: "I agree. Maybe I didn't use the right example, precisely because we're all using it, but the military authority cannot run civil matters in the terrain ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If you turn to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: "... military authority cannot decide on who goes to which house." President replies: "It cannot, but it can maintain order in these transitional periods."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Turning the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Dr. Radic replies: "I agree with you, but where's the problem? The problem is where [sic] the person elected in civil authority is bad, and that is usually the case. Well, not everywhere, we have a good one in Kostajnica but the one in Knin is no good. I don't know where he came from, he's a Serb." The president replies to the question: "He is a Serb?" Dr. Radic replies: "Yes, yes, I was told yesterday that he was a Serb. He's no good for anything." President Tudjman replies: "Okay, replace him." Dr. Radic goes on: "We discussed that as well today. But since this guy is no good, naturally Cermak has to do everything, and then various problems come up ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I think if we turn the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: "The county executive gives up, et cetera, so there's a lot of mess in the terrain. I'm telling you this because I've been through that and seen it all over there." President Tudjman says: "There is no reason for a Serb being there right now." Dr. Radic replies: "Sure, he shouldn't be there." And the president says: "There's a majority of Croats there, so change that." Now -- I'll just wait a moment while that translates.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you agree that the person that President Tudjman and Dr. Radic are talking about is Mr. Pasic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And although in your statement you had said all authorities accepted him and you qualified that to some extent, saying it was more the people you knew in the area, you have, in your statement, said that you understood how the leadership thought. However, this exchange would suggest that, at least with regard to Mr. Pasic, there is exhibited a certain bias against having a Serb in that position in Knin. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to comment on a meeting that I did not attend, because experience teaches me that there are many elements that go into what people say at a particular time in a particular place. But if you ask -- if you are asking me, I will be happy to answer that question, and I will, of course, appreciate what the president said about being brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I take it you agree with me, then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't agree with you. President Tudjman was a man who wanted efficiency. The point here is not that Mr. Pasic is a Serb; the point is that he was inefficient, ineffective. And as at that time people spoke about others in terms of Serb and Croat, it gives the impression that that's the main thing here, which it isn't. The main point here is being able to -- to achieve an effect in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, you don't mention in your statement anywhere about Mr. Pasic being ineffective or inefficient or anything. You actually spend two paragraphs of your statement praising him. Can you explain the absence of your new evaluation on his inefficiency?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was an assessment of why President Tudjman may have said that, and I cannot judge Mr. Pasic's efficiency. I only spoke about the position he found himself in and his psychological and moral traits that -- as I saw them in my contacts with him and based on what I heard from people, mostly ethnic Croats, who considered Mr. Pasic an honest man.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So just to go back a little bit. Despite what the president says in the transcript about an exchange with -- with Dr. Radic saying is he no good, he should be replaced, et cetera, the inefficiency, et cetera, that you attributed to the statement, you're just speculating about that. You don't really know, despite the words that are on the page. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree with the way you're putting it. I knew along which lines he was thinking. There were many situations in the Croatian political life when Mr. Tudjman accepted somebody efficient irrespective of his or her ethnic background. And we are now speaking about a time when it was necessary to react fast, and he decided based on the input he received. There were elements of chaos, there was lack of control, and President Tudjman simply wanted to replace the man in charge. That is how I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: At the time that you were there, August/September 1995, he wasn't replaced, though, was he?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Do you remember Mr. Pasic at all during September 1995 being in Knin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did meet him occasionally, but never in an official meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you said in your statement that you did not speak with President Tudjman in the period leading up to Operation Storm, nor during the period after Operation Storm. You did, however, mention that you had conversations with President Tudjman during an earlier period of time in his office in Zagreb. Can you explain very briefly what period of time you're talking about, that these meetings were happening?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the end of 1993, November to be more precise, up to roughly May 1994. And, later, it happened occasionally at some social events or at tennis matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: In the period leading up to Operation Storm, did you consider yourself a confidant of the president?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered myself that throughout the period. But I also knew that confidence is not sufficient to deal with all things in life. It ask also necessary to know, to have knowledge about these things, and I didn't consider myself a person who could be of assistance to President Tudjman at the time, nor did he hold that opinion. I'm speaking about military issues or other issues, because I know nothing about military things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Moving away from military things for a second, correct me if I'm wrong, Mr. Dodig, but in your statement you seem to base your understanding of President Tudjman's position vis-a-vis Serbs by reference to his -- his soul, which, according to you, apparently revealed a more emotional man at first glance. And my question, Mr. Dodig, is, whether during your interactions with President Tudjman, you ever heard Serbs in Croatia referred to as a threat or a strategic threat, or as a cancer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never in such a way. It did happen that there was talk about the problem of the Serbs and how the state can be consolidated. But never were there -- there was anything pointing to a possible negative attitude of President Tudjman toward the Serbs as an ethnic community. When terms such as "cancer" were used, they didn't apply to all Serbs but only those who impede the consolidation of Croatian statehood, and certainly a much greater number of Serbs in Croatia then lived and still live in towns where there was no imminent threat of war. So we are -- I'm now speaking about territories where the Croatian state had no control, and President Tudjman has a rational and normal attitude toward the Serbian community in Croatia as an integral part of the civic body or civil body of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But I am correct, you have heard the term "cancer" being applied to at least some Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. This has come up --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. I mean that question -- well, the question's been answered but it's the context of any comment on that regard that the Chamber has heard is extremely important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- and I just point to Dr. Zuzul's testimony on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness, and to that extent I think Mr. Carrier is right asking the witness, the witness explained to us what was meant if the word "cancer" was used. Now therefore it is appropriate to ask the witness when, as far as he knows, that word was used and in what circumstances. Could you give us an example of when the word "cancer" was used in relation to Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never present when such a word was used, so whatever I say would be mere guessing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please refrain from guessing in this courtroom, to explain to us what the word "cancer" would have meant if used in relation to Serbs where you were not present. Even if you were not present, you can have knowledge about such an event, even without being present, we would then like to know. But just to explain the context of the use of the word "cancer" where you say you would be just guessing, is not something that assists the Chamber. Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you said that you were never present when the term "cancer" was used in relation to Serbs. Were you present during the freedom train speech in Knin that President Tudjman gave on the 26th August 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, continuing on on President Tudjman's position on Serbs, in your statement, you say that his position was to -- or in order to encourage Serbs to start loving Croatia, the president was of the view that Serbs had to be given greater rights than other Croatian citizens, and you call that positive discrimination. Mr. Dodig, this Chamber has received evidence that President Tudjman was openly advocating that Croatia should try to entice Croats from abroad, places like Paraguay, Australia, Chile, Germany, and Argentina, to return to Croatia after Operation Storm, in order to re-populate the Krajina; and, at the same time, President Tudjman was also expressing his view that the Serbs that had fled during the operation should not be allowed to return home. Mr. Dodig, my question for you is: Would you agree that contemplating such differential treatment in terms of Croats versus Serbs is very difficult to reconcile with your statement regarding President Tudjman's views that Serbs were an integral part of Croatia, deserving of positive discrimination.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow, I'll try to explain very briefly. President Tudjman, with regard to populating Croatia, invited not only Croats from the countries you mentioned to populate the Krajina but also to go to the islands that are sparsely populated, to go to Lika, and Croatia is -- has a small -- small population compared to its size, only about 4 million, 4 and a half million. President Tudjman said to me explicitly and used the term, understanding the political significance of the Serbs in Croatia, their historic role in the Croatian state, and the attitude of the world when it comes to Serbs and Croatia. So he most certainly did not have a negative attitude toward them. Whether he liked them or not isn't for me to speculate about. But he wanted the Serbs in Croatia to feel like citizens that are an integral part of that state, and in order -- or to enable them to feel that way in this young country consolidating itself, he wanted to give them greater rights than other citizens of Croatia. To mention an example, the voting right at elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, can I just ask you about something you just said, because I'm going to suggest to that you you're contradicting yourself. You said -- in relation to President Tudjman: "So he most certainly did not have a negative attitude towards them." Meaning Serbs. And then you go on to say: "Whether he liked them or not isn't for me to speculate about." Now, can you explain how those things, two statements can hang together, because it seems that you, in fact, in the first sentence are speculating, given your second sentence?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I disagree with you. You don't have -- you don't need to have a positive attitude towards someone if -- only if you like them, because liking somebody is an emotional category; whereas, a positive attitude is a rational one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say you really don't have any knowledge of President Tudjman's personal views on Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cannot be said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, would this assist the Chamber? The witness is clearly explaining to us that whether you like someone or not you can nevertheless take a positive approach to a person or a group, and that you can treat someone fairly well even if you don't like him. Think about doctors in hospital who would treat people they do not like at all but treat them from a medical point of view in a perfect way. Therefore, you are seeking apparently something I have difficulties to follow. There is another matter. You asked the witness, and that is how this line of questioning apparently started, you asked the witness whether the -- whether the differential treatment, as you put to the witness, differential treatment, Croats versus Serbs, whether that is difficult to reconcile with the statement of this witness regarding President Tudjman's views that Serbs were an integral part of Croatia. Now the witness answered extensively that question but not really because the answer came down to there -- I do not believe that there was such a differential treatment. Whether to discuss the consistency of certain views, if you disagree on what these views are, doesn't make that such sense. You see, apparently, inconsistency in what the witness says and what you deduce from the testimony we've heard until now. The witness clearly does not accept that that evidence reflects what actually was the truth, and there it stops. And then to hear why he disagrees on a factual basis on your question that we find already in his statement. So the witness answer effectively is, I do not accept your proposition that there's any evidence that could be believed which would reflect such a differential treatment. Let's leave it to that, because this Chamber will finally has to determine whether or not there is credible evidence in relation to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, do you recall what date it was in August 1995 when you first arrived in Knin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say for certain, it was a few days after the liberation of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And in your statement, you -- you seem to indicate that you arrived a few days before you attended the UN camp with General Cermak on the 9th of August. So would it be fair to say it was some time around the 7th of August or so? I mean, just to put it in a ballpark; I know you can't be exact.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, let's say it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And when you arrived Knin, in your statement you describe being out on the street for one or two hours. And you report seeing a joyous atmosphere, people crying with joy, not very many damaged buildings. You do, however, note that there was much disorder. Specifically you say you saw some garbage. My question for you, Mr. Dodig, is, upon arriving in Knin and over the course of the next few days, did you notice any of the following things: Number one, a large number of HV members in the town?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of persons in uniform, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: What about damage caused by shelling to civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mostly walked down the main street in Knin, and there was no severe damage there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Did you notice any evidence of looting by HV members?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw broken shop windows, but evidence of looting, especially by Croatian soldiers, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: What about people in uniform, Croatian Army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It -- it was day-time, and I didn't see anyone looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Any evidence of arson?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Knin itself. I had come from the direction of Drnis, and I saw smoke from afar. But what was burning, whether it was hay or grass or houses, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, this Chamber has received evidence that following Operation Storm's shelling campaign, that the town of Knin itself over the next few days had many HV soldiers present, that there were HV members looting in Knin, that there was arson happening in Knin, and that there were signs of destruction to civilian structures. In light of the evidence before the Chamber on those points, are you able to explain how it is that you didn't see any of those things?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I'm certain that on main street, where I moved about, there was no severe destruction, and it's hard for me to say whether there was more destruction in some other parts of town where I didn't go.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, I want to review a part of your statement with you. Then I'm going to ask you some questions about it. If I could direct your attention to paragraph 19 of your statement, which is on page 11 in the English and 10 in the B/C/S. Second half of that paragraph, you state: "But that was a time when people from all parts of Croatia came, and I think that is why things we did not want happened. I am sure that they were not members of the Croatian Army, although they were wearing uniforms, but everyone" -- sorry, "everybody was wearing a uniform at the time." And then in the next paragraph, paragraph 20, you go on to state: "In my opinion, Mr. Cermak did not know about the crimes either." Mr. Dodig, your reference to "things we did not want to happen," do you mean crimes like arson and looting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement I gave was based on my knowledge and the facts that I learned during all these years since Operation Storm and not based on what I knew at that time about the crimes, because, at that time, I knew nothing. I only learned of them in the following years. When I spoke -- or, rather, that I didn't speak to Mr. Cermak about crimes because I didn't know about them, I -- I based that on fact because I think that Mr. Cermak would have told me if he had known. So it is natural not to speak about something you don't even know exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, in your statement, in fairness, you didn't say you didn't think General Cermak knew about the crimes either because he would have told you about them had they been happening. You just say: "In my opinion, Mr. Cermak did not know about the crimes either," which, again, contradicts what you said, where you don't speak about things you don't know? Are you saying you just don't know if General Cermak knew about the crimes or are you guessing he didn't know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that in my opinion he didn't know, because I suppose that he would have shared it with me if he had known. But I didn't know of the crimes at that time. I clearly said that I learned about them later. And what does later mean. After five or six months, after a year or two, I learned some facts, read the papers, et cetera, from which it follows that there had been crimes. But, at the time we're speaking about, I didn't know of any crimes. I have seen no dead bodies for me to start wondering what happened, because there weren't any dead bodies where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dodig, would it surprise you, then, that General Cermak himself has told Prosecution investigators that he was aware that members of the HV had committed crimes during this period, which included looting, burning, and killing. And you mentioned reading newspapers later on, but even during this time, in September 1995, General Cermak appeared in the media talking about crimes having been committed. Does that surprise you at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Cermak is an honest man, and he said what he had found out to be true. When I talked to him during several visits to Knin, we discussed these things, and he said nothing of the sort. So what you are saying does not contradict what I say. Because, at that moment, he wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you again now say, At that moment he wasn't aware of it. Let's stick to the facts --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose. I suppose he didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I -- what you know is what you may have discussed with Mr. Cermak. Let's avoid to draw conclusions. What you can say for a fact is what you discussed. What he told you or whether there is any other fact that would indicate such knowledge. Let stick to the facts primarily and not draw conclusions, because that creates most of the possible confusion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I just may raise a matter, I hope the Court finds it helpful. I think the speculation is inherent in the nature of the question that was asked when he is asked to comment upon something that was said on another occasion without any reference to time or other matters. But it's -- it's inherent. I think it is almost inviting a witness to speculate. If I was asking a question in that way, I would anticipate that it would come in that form, that the witness would comment on something that he wasn't a party to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I to some extent agree with you, but, of course, part of the basis for such questions - and perhaps it would be wiser for Mr. Carrier not to be lured into that position - is in the answers, is in the statement of the witness himself. He says, In my opinion, I believe, et cetera, et cetera, and then, of course, we have already a basis for getting confused, confused between what the witness knows for a fact and what the witness believes, what the opinion of the witness is. Mr. Carrier, this is a witness of fact, and let's focus on that, and perhaps it would be wise if the witness said, This is my opinion, you can try to explore the factual based for such an opinion, as I just did, and as I did before, rather than to discuss the accuracy of the opinion. The opinion may be right, the opinion may be wrong. What we're interested in are the knowledge of this witness of the facts, and on the basis of those facts, the Chamber will draw the conclusions whether they are the same, or whether they are different from the conclusions drawn by this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, is it fair to say that you had quite limited contact with General Cermak during your time in Knin during August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, in fact, in your statement you said that during your time in Knin, you only met with General Cermak three or four times and specifically you mentioned the first meeting in his office when you arrived; second meeting when you went to the UN camp with him on the 9th of August; and -- additionally you mentioned having gone to one meeting that General Cermak had and addressed the people present. Is that the sum total of your contact with him, or do you have any other specific recollection of any other time you met with General Cermak in Knin during the period?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if there's any point in mentioning that every time I came, I went to greet him and that was all. There was no substantial meeting at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So, just to be clear, you can't think of another time other than those three examples I just gave you. Is that fair? Other than saying when you came back to Knin on occasion, you'd greet him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And when you left Knin during August and September 1995, how -- how long were you away? Was it for a day, or for a week?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You said that when you came back to Knin you would greet him as well. So "coming back" presumes that you left. And, in fact, I'm putting it to you, you weren't in Knin the whole time. So I'm interested in how many days you actually spent in Knin during August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer in days, but I'm sure that I went six or seven times to a refugee camp. I saw the refugee camp as the focus of my work and I tried to resolve problems there, because I think that was the only structured environment in which you could do anything in an organised way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You didn't only just go to the refugee camp. You went to Zagreb as well, didn't you, to attend cabinet meetings?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did go back to Zagreb, but there were no substantial meetings to discuss that topic. There were current affairs that I had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, again, Mr. Carrier clearly seeks information about presence and absence in Knin. You give us a tiny little bit of information about -- you say, I went to a refugee camp. I don't know whether that was 10 kilometres from Knin or 100 kilometres from Knin, which could serve to better know for how long you were away. You tell us about the importance of being in a refugee camp. Mr. Carrier says, But you also went to Zagreb. Then you start telling us about the importance of the meetings in Zagreb. What Mr. Carrier wants to know is, during this period of time, how often and how long you were in Knin; and how often and how long you were elsewhere. So if could you please focus your answer on what is asked, rather than to deal with all kind of matters in which Mr. Carrier has not yet showed any interest to be informed about. So could you tell us, month of August, how often were you away, and where was that camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to be as precise as I can in my answer. The refugee camp in Knin was located roughly 800 metres, one kilometre from Knin so it was very, very close. My workplace was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, in terms of returning to Knin, when you were in the refugee camp, you were actually in Knin, perhaps not exactly in town but within one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes [In English] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So Mr. Carrier started asking about when you say, When I returned to Knin, the refugee camp was more or less in Knin. How long did you stay there? A couple of hours, or one or more days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, from two to three, three and a half hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now Mr. Carrier apparently wants to know what you meant when you said, When I returned to Knin, where you had been. Now, did you include in that answer your absence for a couple of hours, going to the refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke mostly to people in the street. I know on two occasions I visited also the hospital --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Dodig.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- because I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, again, please try to understand what is asked from you. It was about meeting Mr. Cermak when you returned to Knin. Now, did you refer to meeting Mr. Cermak when you had been in the refugee camp; or did you refer to meeting Mr. Cermak when you had been in Zagreb for whatever reason? That's what Mr. Carrier is interested to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- the actual question was -- because I was watching this as there was a couple. I'm interested in how many days you actually spent in Knin. I think the question had departed from Mr. Cermak to how many days in -- in Knin. I hope that assists Your Honour and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but how many days you are in Knin is directly related to how many days you're not in Knin. And apparently the focus initially was on the frequency of contacts with Mr. Cermak, which were described in terms of, When I returned to Knin. Mr. Carrier, is that what you --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- sought information about. Now let's try really strictly to stick to facts and preferably the facts that you are asked about, and then if you know them, tell us; if you don't know them, tell us as well. Please proceed, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, during the months of August and September of 1995, how many days did you spend in Knin itself; if you know?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot be mathematically precise. I can say seven or eight days. That's how many days I spent in Knin. When I say "day," I mean from 9.00 a.m. to around 2.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And other than these seven days, where were you the rest of the time during August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was working in my workplace. I had annual leave and some other things to attend to at the hospital where I was also working.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And that's in Split, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So in your statement, all the observations and evaluations that you make of General Cermak, his authority, what happens at the meetings, whether or not he can issue orders, that's based on the few days that you were in Knin up to seven days during August and September 1995. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was mainly in August. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And because the refugee camp is basically in Knin, that you were going to because you said that was your primary focus, I take it that your visits to those -- to the refugee camp was happening during the seven days that you were actually physically in Knin during August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, in view of the statement of the witness -- When you are talking about the refugee camp, what actually are you talking about? Are you talking about the UN compound; or are you talking about any other refugee camp? Mr. Dodig, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The UN base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Then we know where it is. Then if you would have used that word - and I'm not blaming for you for choosing your own - then I would not have had to ask about the distance. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So in your statement you discuss having attended an open-door meeting with General Cermak. Is it fair to say it's just one meeting that you went to in that respect?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, but I have to say this. Very often terminological differences create great problems. When I say meeting, I mean when I came to Knin to call on Mr. Cermak. It was not a proper meeting. Mr. Cermak was so busy, people were coming and going all the time. That's why I called it open doors. It was so hectic that there was no time, no opportunity for any meaningful conversation. Mr. Cermak was often embarrassed that he had no more time to give me and talk to me properly. He would just say a few sentences and say, I'm sorry about this, but let's try to -- to do what needs to be done. There was no meeting in the sense that there was an agenda, people attending a proper discussion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I suggest to you that when this was just a brief encounter that you use the expression, I briefly saw him, and if there was any meeting with an agenda, you would then that call that a meeting so that we avoid confusion for the remaining time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Dodig, you are actually talking about a brief contact with General Cermak when you say that you didn't notice any military police or civilian police at -- isn't really a meeting but it's a brief contact between you and General Cermak. Is that what you're talking about in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And is it fair to say, then, in your statement where you're talking about General Cermak issuing orders to people, that relates also to these periods of time when you're having brief contact with General Cermak. You just don't see him during those brief contacts issuing orders or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were very brief moments, true. But even in those brief moments, he would contact several people, to whom he would issue certain instructions, I would say, rather than orders, as to what needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But you don't actually know whether or not General Cermak was issuing orders to anybody. You don't actually have knowledge of that. You're just talking about the brief interactions you had with him.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And is it the same when you say that you didn't think that General Cermak understood military hierarchy or that he wasn't really a member of the military. That was just based on your brief interactions with him during those seven days that you spent in Knin, not on anything else. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And going back because it wasn't apparent in your statement, when you talk about not seeing much destruction in Knin or looting or crimes committed by HV, this is limited to the certain days obviously that were in Knin, which you can't actually identify precisely, other than, perhaps, the 9th of August, 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you didn't actually make it clear in your statement that you were only in Knin for seven days during August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know it mattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if I could just return to -- to something you said before. When I raised the issue of having attended a cabinet in Zagreb, you said that you had attended, is that right, you had attended cabinet meetings during August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended meetings within the office that I was in charge of, not cabinet meetings. There was one cabinet meeting held in Knin itself where I was invited and I went. But did I not attend other cabinet meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: At the cabinet meeting that you did attend, you said before that you didn't talk about anything do with the issues in Knin. Is that fair? Because I was confused by something you said there. I'll just try to find it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So I take it, then, you wouldn't have been -- your name wouldn't be on a transcript during a cabinet meeting where you discuss four different types of Serbs that remain in the Krajina in August 1995; where you discuss certain problems; where you discuss the number of Serbs left in the Krajina. That doesn't ring a bell at all?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know it's slightly early, but this is -- the next document is the one that we had trouble uploading and it's the last thing I will be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and may I take it that if we have a break of 25 minutes, that then the problem will be resolved?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I would love to say yes, but let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm being told yes, it will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'm expressing a certain amount of doubt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- already saving your position if it turns out not to be the case. That's the only document you still wanted to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I may also have a few brief questions about the first two I tried to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber wants to avoid that we come back here and wait for another 10 or 15 minutes to find that the problems were not resolved. Could you -- we will have a break of 25 minutes and we'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00. But if, for whatever reason, you'll not be able to put on the screen what you want to put on the screen, we'd like to be informed before we enter the courtroom. We'll have a break, and we will resume at - I give you five more minutes - five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you even had more time, due to all kind of other things Judges of this Chamber had to do during the break. Apologies for the late start. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Registrar, could we please have document number 65 ter 7431 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dodig, what is going to appear on the front of you [sic] is a document which are the minutes of the 260th Closed Session of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And for Your Honours and my friends, there's only six pages that have been translated into English and unfortunately it wasn't the cover page, given the short turnaround time. But I'll suggest what it says to Mr. Dodig and he can agree or disagree. That may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: But looking at the front page, Mr. Dodig, is that what it says, that this is the 260th Closed Session of the Croatian government, and then below that, it lists the date of the 23rd of August, 1995, and starts to list the various participants in the session?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess that must be correct. I didn't attend that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we could just turn to the second page in B/C/S, please. And if we go near the top. In the indented paragraph in bold at the top, Mr. Dodig, your name is mentioned there, Dr. Dodig.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Does that refresh your memory about a session that started at 11.05 a.m., on the 23rd of August, 1995, and whether or not you actually attended that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. If it says here, then I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, it's only five lines back that you said that you didn't attend that meeting. Could I ask to you very carefully think about the answers you are giving. I do understand that you focussed on what you saw on the cover sheet. But if you rely on any document to -- when giving your answer, would you -- and that was more or less what I found to you say; that is, that since your name was not there, you must not have attended that meeting, whereas on the second page you saw your name and said, Well, then I must have been there. That we know exactly what are conclusions based upon reading documents and what is your own recollection. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Registrar, if we could turn to page 14 in the B/C/S, please, and remaining on page 1 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You see at the top of the page, Mr. Dodig, your name appears and I'm suggesting to that the reason that is, is because it indicates that you're the one speaking here, because these were recorded meetings that had been transcribed. And if we look at -- in the English version halfway down where it begins with the words, "Of course" - this is you speaking - which, again, in Croatian is also halfway down the page. It basically corresponds and beginning with the word -- I'll mispronounce it but it is "dakako." In this section, Mr. Dodig, of the minutes, you're talking and you're actually talking about that you're concluding that there is four categories of people, that is Serbs that remained in the liberated areas after Operation Storm, and you give us a breakdown of what those groups consist of. One is those that remained in the villages and hamlets. The next are Serbs that were the UNCRO barracks in Knin. Then you talk about the Serbs that are in collection or investigation centres, which is the third category. The fourth is in Western Slavonia, which finishes off at the bottom of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I have an inquiry. I'm sorry, counsel, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I look at this document with the 65 ter number, and I look at this transcript with my colleague, Mr. Misetic, and I don't want to speak for my other colleagues but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it a matter you're raising at this moment that can be raised in the presence of the witness? I don't know what's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it can be. It has to do with disclosure under Rule 68 subdivision (2) of all relevant information, and it appears to us collectively that we have never seen this document before, albeit it clearly falls into Rule 68 subdivision (2) as relevant matter. And the question I ask my learned friend across the well is why it has not been disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the first question is whether it has been disclosed --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and then if not, why not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, my apologies. My apologies. I took a look with Mr. Misetic and my Case Manager, Ms. Katalinic, and we don't have it disclosed. Now I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the basis for you is that you have no knowledge of any disclosure, so we first seek to verify that. And then if there was no disclosure we'll try to find out what the reasons were. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For our part, Your Honour, this has not been disclosed. This witness has been on our witness list for some considerable time, on the 65 ter list and then as a scheduled witness. There is supposed to have been Rule 68 disclosure in this case. We have made a number of complaints on several occasions about that failing to take place, but I have been able to track a very important reference to my client in this document that I read as being totally exculpatory on an important issue in this case. I am very, very concerned. What is happening here is a document is being sprung up into court. This witness is asked whether he can remember something or not 15 years ago. He is then asked questions. He's then said, Ah, here is your name, so you must have been there. He has got to read the document. He should have been able to read this document whilst we were interviewing him and confirming his 92 ter statement as one of those documents that might be relevant in the case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm stopping you. Let's first try to establish whether there is agreement about the non-disclosure so that we have that for a fact before we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is not on the EDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: On the issue of disclosure, it was disclosed under the RFA 750 in March 2008. It was disclosed on March 6th, 2008, on a CD. ERN range 0614-2565-0614-3142. And if I could perhaps address the other issues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we have a few matters. First, whether it was disclosed. I would invite -- there seems to be disagreement about whether it was disclosed, yes or no. So, therefore, it needs to be verified whether it was disclosed. The second issue is whether it was disclosed specifically also under Rule 68 (i), that is, disclosed as exculpatory material, or whether it was just disclosed in the EDS system. From your answer, I did not understand, Mr. Carrier, that it was specifically disclosed as exculpatory material, which raises another matter, which is whether it is exculpatory material; therefore, we'd have to rely on what Mr. Kay found to be of an exculpatory nature. These are the issues I think we're dealing with at this moment. How we will proceed in verifying whether it was disclosed or not, Mr. Carrier now gave further details about disclosure. Could -- is there a possibility that you verify that right away or should we give you an opportunity first to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The machines are grinding as we speak, Your Honour, to check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, like our brains, Mr. Kay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one last comment on this with regard to the disclosure, and we are checking these -- this range, but we also ask whether or not it has been -- it was disclosed in English, as the OTP is required to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, in what language was it disclosed? In view of the fact that you were still working on the translations, it might not have been already March 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: My understanding is it was disclosed in B/C/S, hence the fact that we're waiting for the translation today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you are waiting for the translation since March or?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, no, my understanding is that there's not a rule that requires it to be disclosed in English, that it just be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rule 68 (ii) you'd say doesn't need to be translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- however exculpatory material.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the decisions I wanted to read, and I don't know whether we find time to read them in its entirety, but the Chamber has decided to grant the requests for videolink, so that hurdle doesn't exist anymore. Now, I also inform the parties that, at this very moment, everyone is working hard to see whether this can be done, so there is no problem in accepting the idea, but the practicalities are rather complex, because there are competing videolinks on these same dates scheduled, which requires that both the Victims and Witness Section and Court Management Services have to consider whether they have staff available to do this all at the same time, or to re-schedule the court schedule either for this Chamber or for the other Chambers which want to use a videolink simultaneously. So that is a rather complex, practical problem at this moment. It seems that nothing opposes adopting the suggested solution, if that can be done. That's the main problem at this moment. I can't give you any results yet. We have to wait until all those involved have -- have made their efforts to see whether this suggested videolink can fit into the programme. Any comments in this respect? If not, then I'd like now to read the two decisions. We would then have a break, and that would give additional time for Mr. Dodig, and even if you don't want to listen to the decisions, but, rather, spent consulting people out of this courtroom elsewhere, the Chamber would fully understand that. And then, at least, we have had some additional time to prepare for what will happen after the break. I start with a decision on protective measures and a video-conference link for Witness IC-1. On the 14th of September, 2009, the Cermak Defence filed a motion requesting the trial-related protective measures of face and voice distortion and pseudonym for Witness IC-1. The Cermak Defence also requested that the evidence of Witness IC-1 be given via video-conference link. On the 17th of September, 2009, the Prosecution filed its response, indicating that it did not object to either of the requests. The Gotovina Defence and the Markac Defence did not respond. The Chamber will first address the request for protective measures. As has been held in previous decisions, the party seeking protective measures must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. As the Chamber set out in its recent decision on protective measures for Witness 13 on the 8th of June, 2009, it should be considered that even though the granting of protective measures is, and should be, the exception to the rule of a public trial, the threshold for when it should be granted cannot be set too high. For example, to exclude persons who have not experienced threats or harassment would defy the purpose of the measures; namely, protection from risks that might occur as a result of the testimony. Witness IC-1 is a Croatian Serb currently residing with his family in Croatia. He has expressed concerns for himself and his family as he believes his testimony could cause hostile reactions in the Serb community -- Serb community of his home town. The witness is expected to testify about how the Croatian authorities treated him after Operation Storm. Recently, the witness learned of threats and harassment directed against another Defence witness, a Serb living in the same town, also testifying in this case and on similar events. This person has already been granted protective measures by the Chamber. Although Witness IC-1 has not experienced any threats directed against him or his family, the Chamber considers that there's a risk that his testimony may antagonise persons in his immediate surroundings, and that he therefore might suffer similar threats or harassment as the witness referred to above. For these reasons, the Chamber finds that the Cermak Defence has demonstrated an objectively grounded risk as to the security and welfare of Witness IC-1, should it become known that he has given evidence before this Tribunal. The Chamber therefore grants the protective measures of face and voice distortion and pseudonym. Even though not requested by the Cermak Defence, the Chamber further grants private session for portions of the testimony that could reveal the witness identity. The Chamber will now address the request for testimony via video-conference link. According to Rule 81 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Chamber may order that the proceedings be conducted by way of video-conference link if it is consistent with the interests of justice. This standard is met, if, first, the witness is unable or has good reasons to be unwilling to come to the seat of the Tribunal; second, the witness's testimony is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the requesting party to proceed without it; and, third, the accused are not prejudiced in the exercise of their rights to confront the witness. The witness, who is 79 years old, has informed the Cermak Defence that he suffers from a serious form of a heart arrythmia and colon cancer. The witness recently had an operation and is currently undergoing treatment which further aggravates his condition. Although no confirming medical records have been presented, and in the absence of objections from the Prosecution and the other parties, the Chamber is satisfied that the witness's advanced age and physical condition render him unable to travel to the Tribunal to testify. Having been notified about the substance of the witness's anticipated testimony, the Chamber is further satisfied that it is sufficiently important to make it unfair for the Cermak Defence to proceed without it. Finally, the Chamber finds that neither party is prejudiced in the exercise of their right to confront Witness IC-1, if the witness appears via video-conference link. The parties, none of whom objected to the motion, will all be provided the opportunity to cross-examine the witness. Therefore, the Chamber finds that it is consistent with the interests of justice to grant the Cermak Defence's request to hear Witness IC-1's testimony via video-conference and grants the request, pursuant to Rule 81 bis. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on protective measures and proceedings via video-conference for Witness IC-1. I now move on to the delivery of the Chamber's decision on the Cermak Defence's motion for video-conference link for Witness IC-2. On 14th of September, the Cermak Defence filed a motion requesting that the evidence of Witness IC-2 be given via video-conference link. On the 28th of September, 2009, the Prosecution filed its response indicating that it did not object to the request. The Gotovina Defence and the Markac Defence did not respond. According to Rule 81 bis of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, a Chamber may order that the proceedings be conducted by way of video-conference link if it is consistent with the interests of justice. This standard is met, if, first, the witness is unable or has good reasons to be unwilling to come to the seat of this Tribunal; second, the witness's testimony is sufficiently important to make it unfair to the requesting party to proceed without it; and, third, the accused are not prejudiced in the exercise of their rights to confront the witness. Witness IC-2 is 83 years old. The Cermak Defence has submitted that his health is frail and that he suffers from asthma. Recently the witness was treated at the local hospital. His doctor told a member of the Cermak Defence that the witness's present condition was caused by stress relating to threats he received in connection to his testimony before the Tribunal. Although no confirming medical records have been presented, and in the absence of objections from the Prosecution and the other parties, the Chamber is satisfied that the witness's advanced age and physical condition render him unable to travel to the Tribunal to testify. Having been notified about the substance of the witness's anticipated testimony, the Chamber is further satisfied that it is sufficiently important as to make it unfair for the Cermak Defence to proceed without it. Finally, the Chamber finds that neither party is prejudiced in the exercise of their right to confront Witness IC-2, if the witness appears via video-conference link. The parties, none of whom objected to the motion, will all be provided with the opportunity to cross-examine the witness. Consequently, the Chamber finds that it is consistent with the interests of justice to grant the Cermak Defence's request to hear Witness IC-2's testimony via video-conference link and therefore grants the motion, pursuant to Rule 81 bis. And this concludes the Chamber's decision on proceedings via video-conference link for Witness IC-2.
