utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could have Exhibit D426 on the screen, please. And I'll do my best to work from that, because that is already in evidence. If we could turn to page 9 in the English, please. Or perhaps actually if we could turn to page 8 first, and page 14 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you can see this is the document that you had a chance to look at. Your name appears at the top. I take it, having had a chance to review this now, are you -- are you in a position to change your mind with regard to something I asked you before, that you actually went to a cabinet meeting, that you talked about four different categories of Serbs left in the Krajina, that you discussed certain problems, and that you also discussed the number of Serbs that remained in the Krajina, now that you've had a chance to look at it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: So was it just that you forgot that you had done that or can you explain how it is that you -- first off that you --

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Dodig, you were asked a very specific question. First, whether you had attended the cabinet meeting; and you said first no, and then you said yes, you had. Then you were asked explicitly whether or not you discussed certain things; you said no. Can you -- I'm just wondering if you can explain. Is it just lack of memory about certain events that happened or ...

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I admit that I have been imprecise, sir, but so have you. We are talking here about a cabinet meeting and not an office meeting. I do not remember everything that happened 15 years ago, and if there are certain imprecisions, then, I will do my best to -- to reconstruct what has happened. And I will certainly speak only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could turn to page 9 in the English version, which -- which is page 15, I believe, in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dodig, on this page in English, halfway down, where you talk about specific problems in relation to the UNCRO barracks in Knin, you are describing a situation which I'm going to put to you sounds problematic. In fact, you say that there's wounded people there, and the overall situation at the point referred to as the hospital is problematic from the point of view of health care. And then you go on about providing beds for some adults and some childrens -- for some children. I'm asking you if you can explain those comments in the cabinet meeting, in relation to the statement you gave, where you say, at paragraph 16, that after a few visits to the UNCRO camp, you say that the situation was completely calm and that none of the people showed any interest in talking to you, and before that you describe basically a medical situation that isn't problematic at all. Can you explain why it is that the cabinet meeting reflects a different interpretation of the events?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember how much I spoke at the cabinet meeting and how it was translated, about things that happened or about the situation as it was at the time. But, certainly, my visit to the UNCRO refugee camp, as we called it, was such that I detected the situation, I established what it was like, and -- at the humanitarian and why not say political level, and what I said here is a result of a -- this information that I learned. And on the following day, we sent a truckload of medical items to Knin. I knew what the general policy was and what -- how we should behave in such situations. And my interpretation of the situation, as it was, and even at the cabinet meeting where I spoke about the four categories of Serbs, these are my arbitrary -- this is my arbitrary classification. It's not based on any expert finds or scientific research. I focussed on this because there were a great many problems. The people were disinterested because they had received what they wanted, and later on, it all depended on their own decisions, whether they would leave camp together in any direction -- well, some of them later did go abroad. And when I look at this report and when I see how we spoke and when I see the reactions in the cabinet, I'm still proud of what we did, because we didn't see them as enemies but as people who needed help. So I do not know what exactly to answer to you. Do ask me more precisely, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, would you please focus your answer on what is asked. But, apparently, Mr. Carrier, Mr. Dodig has difficulties, so could you please focus his attention to what you would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Basically I just wanted to know, Mr. Dodig, why is it different in terms of what you are saying in the cabinet versus what you say in your statement. That's all I want to know on that -- on that point.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask you to point out these essential differences to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I'll take that answer as you don't see any essential differences and I will move on. On page 16 of your statement, halfway down that paragraph, and near the bottom of the first paragraph on page 9 in English, you're discussing particular problems in the barracks, the UNCRO barracks, and one of the things you talk about is presence of media and the problem of the -- what you call the so-called informative interview, i.e., the manner in which the people who, in a way, participated in the armed rebellion against Croatia would be separated from those who didn't. The next paragraph goes on: "On the one hand, it is General Cermak's very good wish to solve it as soon as possible, while, on the other hand, there's a tendency within the barracks itself that anyone who wants to leave is free to leave." My question is: What you are talking about there is that General Cermak was insisting that there be interviews of people in the camp before they be allowed to leave. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, General Cermak said that he had to speak to the camp commander and agree with him what to do and how to resolve the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: That's with regard to the interviews, though, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 17 in the B/C/S. And if we can start -- which is this second paragraph appearing on page 17 in the B/C/S, which is the final paragraph on page 9 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: You're quoted as saying here, Mr. Dodig, that -- and these are the people inside of the UNCRO camp: "As for their attitude on leaving Croatia, most of them wishes to leave, approximately 70 per cent of them, and there's also a smaller number of those who cannot decide as their decision depends on the fact whether their house is preserved or not, whether it is burnt or not, and very often, as a pre-condition for making the decision, they asked to be allowed to go outside and convince themselves of the condition of their property." You don't mention that in your statement anywhere, that the people that you were talking to in the UNCRO camps were predicating their decision on whether to leave, or at least some of them, on whether or not their house had been burnt down. Can you explain why you didn't mention that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I failed to mention many things in my statement because otherwise my testimony would go on for days. I can mention dozens of examples of helping people and taking them outside, but I didn't consider it necessary for this trial. When people said they wanted to leave, they were scared, on the one hand, and, on the other hand, they were curious to see what had happened. They were mostly people who were not from Knin itself but from the surroundings. So a period of time was necessary to enable them to see it, but there were examples of people who had left and decided on their own to stay. And perhaps another detail, often in conversations with these people, the issue wasn't whether there were people there who had remained and felt innocent, it wasn't an issue whether they would stay for political reasons, but simply for existential reasons, economic reasons, whether they would have anything to live off --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, I was just pausing -- I was just pausing to let the translation finish, not to invite to you answer more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 19 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Where are you speaking and the bottom of page 10 in the English. You're quoted, Mr. Dodig, as estimating that the number of Serbs that remained in the former occupied territories was between 2.000 and 2500 citizens of Serb nationality. You also didn't mention those numbers in your statement anywhere. Can you explain why that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply didn't consider that an important piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Dodig, earlier today when I had asked you about certain public statements had you made regarding the Tribunal, you said that you didn't speak about the work of the Tribunal, but, rather, its motives. And I'm going to suggest to you that you said more than -- you made comments that were more than just about the motives. You said, and this is document 65 ter 7428, which we started to look at before it wouldn't be called up. This, just to be clear, is an article that appeared in Slobodna Dalmacija on January 30th, 2001, where some comments were attributed to you, and I will read what you it says in one respect. You say: "'The Hague Tribunal is a political Tribunal. It has money, power, media, and army, but it does not have a moral power, and it will make a faux pas because of that sooner or later,' warned Dodig, saying that judgements are worthless unless they are perceived as righteous." Do you have any recollection, Mr. Dodig, of making that type of statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did speak often about the way I see the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, but I do not remember when I said this, and I'm positive that I never authorised such a text. What you said may be a free interpretation of a journalist. But if you are interested in my opinion, I will -- I will present it, but I consider this to be a free interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this: Do you agree with the sentiment expressed, in terms of what I just read to you? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only sentiment but I certainly never said that the Tribunal in The Hague had an army, because that is nonsense. There are many things we can talk about, but a man can change his opinion based on the facts that he learns. Whatever I said in 2001 doesn't mean that I would say the same thing today, due to the information that I learned in the meantime and that effect my -- the way I see a certain problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, Mr. Carrier is asking you whether the sentiment in the quote is what you said. And then you started explaining that you changed your mind and that you would have never said that the Tribunal had an army. Is that to be understood as that the sentiment, apart from the army part, was, in 2001, your opinion, and that you changed it since then? I'm trying to understand your answer. Because Mr. Carrier is trying to focus on what you said at the time; whereas, you are saying, I don't think about this anymore in this way. Does that mean that the sentiment, as expressed, apart from the army part, is more or less reflecting your thoughts at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the issue of how I see the Tribunal in The Hague is something I would need much more time to elaborate than just to answer yes or no. So it is practically impossible to give an unambiguous answer to your question. I am actually embarrassed by having to pass judgement on some people who are being tried, and that is the reason why I'm being emotional about this Tribunal. Bearing -- I swore at the beginning of my testimony that I would say the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and I cannot lie either to you or to myself. I have an opinion about this Tribunal, but I don't want this opinion to affect your attitude toward the indictees here. I'm deeply convinced that the bad things that happened after Operation Storm would have been even worse if it hadn't been for these people who were in their respective positions. Speaking about things beyond a time-frame and outside of a certain area is -- will result in not only a different experience but also in wrong conclusions. Both as a human being and a doctor, I'm convinced that those who did bad things that make me shiver, just as any civilised person, not only in Croatia but anywhere in the world, that these people are not sitting here. In every society there are some 15 to 20 per cent of psychopaths and those were the times when such people did bad things, committed crimes, but these people are not the ones sitting here. And that is the reason why I have a such an opinion about this Tribunal, which I value highly, and I believe that it will eventually pass a just judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, could I seek one clarification. You earlier said: "I'm actually embarrassed by having to pass judgement on people being tried." Now, who did you have in mind that would have to pass judgement? Who -- you're embarrassed by us having to pass judgement, or that you, as a witness, would have to pass judgement? What did you mean? I read the sentence again to you. You said: "I'm actually embarrassed by having to pass judgement on people being tried, and that is the reason why I'm going emotional about the Tribunal." The first part of the sentence, could you please explain what you actually meant there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can. Testimonies and the replies that I have to give as a witness and which are often brief result in possible false conclusions, and I feel as part -- part of these people here. If I knew that, at any moment, any one of them, directly or indirectly, by failing to do something, helped to commit criminal deeds anywhere, believe me that I would be unwilling to live in such a country, and I couldn't identify with that society or that time or those people in any way. So the trial they are standing here, I see as a trial I am standing too, and I know what -- how -- how willing I was to sacrifice and what my -- that my motives were humane. I would like to remind everybody of the Jewish proverb that the fate of one person is the fate of the entire world. And that is why I feel this way, and I'm trying to explain it to you. By participating in this trial or in these proceedings, I feel like I'm also involved in trying these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No more questions. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give an opportunity to the parties to put further questions to you, when you said, in this meeting on the 23rd of August that there were wounded people, could you elaborate on who were wounded or what kind of wounds you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement, I mentioned that I had seen wounds, but I did see young people who were covered up to their waist with blankets and they were lying down. I shook their hands, and I concluded that they were only slightly wounded, possibly they were not even -- they didn't even have wounds that were bleeding. And it was in a moral dilemma: Should I react as a doctor or as representative of the Croatian authorities? None of them -- none of those whose hand I shook had a fever. Of course, that isn't anything that I can claim for certain. Everyone had a strong enough -- had -- had enough strength in his hand, and I can say as much, because I have been -- I had been a doctor for decades and I have experience, so I can tell what a case is about when I see it. So I supposed that they had some kind of viruses. But by the way they moved underneath that blanket, I could tell that they had some other problems. I was -- those people were all very young, between 20 and 35 years of age, and even in unrelated conversation with the late Mr. Pupovac, who was the president of that refugee council, who said, If any of these injured needs medical assistance, let me know, and I will see to it. Those are my words and he said, No problem, be assured that we will let you know, if necessary. So these people certainly weren't -- didn't suffer wounds by playing football, and -- as I said at the cabinet meeting. But resolving the situation at that moment would have -- would have had more detrimental consequences than positive ones, at that moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you earlier asked Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig, you asked Mr. Carrier to further explain to you what the inconsistencies would be what you said in this meeting on the 23rd and what you say in your statement. Now, in your statement, first of all, you say they were not wounded; whereas, in the government meeting you are reported to have said that there's wounded people there and that there was a problematic situation as far as health care is concerned. Now, looking at it in the context, and also listening to your answer you just gave, people might think that the inconsistency between what you said in the government and what you said in your statement is the following. That in the statement you present a picture where people are pretending to be sick and to be wounded, and that you are fully aware that they are only trying to hide and that you didn't say anything about that; whereas, in the government meeting the picture created could be understood as a different one, that people were wounded and there was a problematic health-care situation. Now, I think that this is one of the issues Mr. Carrier had on his mind when he asked you to explain the inconsistencies; that is, the picture you give on page 8 in your statement and the words you spoke at the government meeting, could you given an explanation for that. And I'm not inviting you to again tell us what you exactly did; but I'm inviting you to explain the different colour in the two pictures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to explain very briefly. In my statement that I gave to this Tribunal, I did not mention that there were wounded people because I cannot say that for certain. When I spoke at the government session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dodig --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that there were wounded people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I'm going to stop you there. You say you could not establish that there were wounded, so therefore, that's why you gave your statement. Now, your statement - but if it is incorrectly translated, I would like to hear - says they were not wounded; whereas, if I understand your testimony now well, is that you apparently wanted to say, I could not finally establish whether they were wounded or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not see a single wound, but from circumstantial evidence, I thought there were wounds and injuries. But the way a court judges things, in terms of yes or no, I cannot claim anything for certain. I don't have the tangible evidence. But when I say that there are wounded people, and I say it at a government meeting, that sort of obliges those present to respond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- more quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what you're actually saying at this moment - and please correct me when I've misunderstood you -- is there were good reasons to believe that people were wounded, but I could not finally establish whether they were or not. That's approximately what you tell us now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly that's it. And, of course, there are wounds of varying intensity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not asking you to further elaborate on what wounds there are. In your statement, you say, they were not wounded. You do not say, I had every reason to believe that they were wounded but I couldn't establish that. You say they were not wounded, and you then further explain, in direct relation to that, that they were hiding rather than being sick and/or wounded. That creates a totally different picture from what you tell us now. Could you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any point -- at every point in my statement, I say that it's my evaluation. Whatever I'm saying is my perception and my evaluation. When I say here there were no wounded people, I say that because I didn't see any wounds. And precisely because I appreciated the fact that the Court requires positive statements, I could not say that there were any wounded people because I did not see any wounds. What I said was the result of my experience as a physician and the circumstances of that particular situation. Some of those people who were perhaps sick or wounded pretended to be in good health, but I myself pretended that I do not notice. And I said a moment ago that by the way they moved under the bedding, it was obvious they had certain problems and conditions that could have been a result of trauma rather than disease, and this trauma, I believe, they sustained in war operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this belief -- do you have any reason for that, any factual basis for these conclusions, or is it just what you think may be the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that was so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, any wish to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, just a few questions arising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Dr. Dodig, you were asked questions about meeting Mr. Cermak, and just to get the picture, I'd like to ask you some questions about that. You described in your statement about visiting the UN camp with Mr. Cermak on the 9th of August. And I wonder if you're able to tell us as to how long you were with Mr. Cermak on that day.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Relatively briefly. I believe up to an hour in his office. But that doesn't mean that I was with him. We reached the camp, I can't remember how, and then he went to one side to speak to the Military Commander of the camp, and I followed another medical errand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the meeting with the Council of Refugees took how long?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimation, between two and a half and three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that meeting with them, was that a meeting at which both you and Mr. Cermak were at together during that time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I was alone at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you explain how long Mr. Cermak was with you, then, and the Refugee Council when you had discussions with them on this visit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few minutes, perhaps. He greeted them and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the questions that you were asked about other meetings, you referred in your statement that you knew that Mr. Cermak held meetings in his office with representatives of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from many people who came to Knin that they had spoken to Mr. Cermak, but I'd like to find the right term for these interactions. I would call them brief encounters; that would be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked questions about the differences between your perception of the camp when you gave your statement at the closed session of the government on the 23rd of August, which we saw in the transcript, Exhibit D426, with the phrase in your statement: "... the situation was completely calm and none of those people showed interest in talking to me." What did you mean by the expression "the situation was completely calm"? Perhaps you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was calm enough for medical affairs to be under control. Second, they were given the possibility to decide themselves what their next step would be: Leave the camp, or stay. The situation was also calm insofar as a kind of peace reigned, and people were no longer afraid of what might happen the next minute and whether they would be able to leave or not. They had already succeeded in establishing contact with a number of international humanitarian organisations that visited and they had managed to come in touch with their family and perhaps some other people and organisations who were able to give them more assistance than I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dodig. I would like to just talk with you a bit about some of the questions that were asked from my learned friend Mr. Carrier and the quote that he read about this -- this being -- The Hague Tribunal being a political Tribunal. And I take it your opinions and your views on The Hague Tribunal were shaped by what you read and saw and heard coming out of the Tribunal, and statements by its staff. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me bring up on the screen [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Apologies. I can bring up on the screen via Sanction, 65 ter 1D2986. And this is an excerpt from Ms. Florence Hartmann's book, from page 44, 47, and 48, that's been translated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- Mr. Kehoe, let's -- before we start this, if you want to put something to the witness rather than reading a text to him. Mr. Dodig, could I ask your attention, please, not to read at this moment on the screen. You're still -- yes. Could you ask the witness whether he has read the book before we come to any further conclusions on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Ms. Hartmann's book?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not what I suggest but whether he read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, I just -- no, no. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My first question was familiar; my next question did he read it and was he aware of conversation -- well, I'll just ask the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with Ms. Hartmann's book?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Ms. Hartmann published a book and I have read certain excerpts that appeared in our press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, sir, you are aware that that book was translated into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you, likewise, were aware that Ms. Hartmann did a media tour throughout Croatia and excerpts of that book were published in the Croatian press. You are aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And are you aware, sir, of Ms. Hartmann's allegations that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's first ask the witness what he remembers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- from the excerpts, and then if that creates any link, then, of course, we have that link clearly established. If it doesn't create a link then, of course, then we could further see whether it refreshes the witness's memory. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Dodig, in your -- your comments -- excuse me, in the matters of Ms. Hartmann's writings and her speeches, can you tell us basically what you read from that book and specifically what excerpts you read from that book concerning her activities within the Office of the Prosecutor when she was the spokesperson?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this moment I cannot recall any details. Those were excerpts I read in newspapers that were actually journalists' views and interpretations. I am one of those people who hate talking about things they are not perfectly familiar with. I know that Mrs. Hartmann published a book. I know that she was tried for contempt of court, but I cannot recall any details of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you something that refresh your recollection concerning her comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I turn to excerpts from her book, 65 ter 1D2986, that we show via Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, just for my information, you started with what was published, as Mr. Dodig says, views. That was in 2001. That was your starting point of your line of questioning. And then you are apparently exploring on what basis he had formed his opinions. Now, are we talking about the opinions expressed in 2001, or are we talking about the opinions, as he said, had changed his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Hartmann is talking about what happened in 2001. If we contextualise what Hartmann is talking about, is about events in 2001 and prior to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then, of course, it becomes important to know what the witness knows, apart from perhaps later reading it in Ms. Hartmann's book, about what happened in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You understand, I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. The issue that the Prosecution is attempting to say -- and maybe the witness might take his earphones off, so I don't really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we first have to establish whether he speaks any English or not. Some psychiatrists do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You do. Then it is of no use to take your earphones off, Mr. Dodig.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, it may be clear that there's nothing that should not be asked to this witness, but it should always be clear what he knew, at what time, and what could be at the basis of whatever statement, opinion, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the first thing we have to establish what comes to his recollection without the assistance of any refreshment and then after that, we could see whether his recollection, if there is any need to do so, is refreshed by any matter. I would like to have that on the basis of a clear analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- my line of cross is different than articulated by the Chamber. In the line of cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about your line of cross --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No, no, no, but because it's -- because it is -- it is different in the sense of whether or not the witness has read and analysed what Florence Hartmann said. To the extent that he perceived, in 2001, the Tribunal being a political body, and to the extent that his credibility or bias is being attacked by the OTP in that regard, this is showing the Chamber, through this witness, that the -- he was not the only person during this operative time-frame to say that this body was political.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. -- okay. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And that the OTP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, you're then invited to first explore with the witness, without using any book or anything else, to explore what was at the basis of his opinions at that time. And then once we know that, that we could then compare that with other people's opinions at the time. We would then at least know whether what you will put to him as the opinions of others is the same or is different, and, therefore, we first have to explore what was at the basis of his opinions. Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could move into private session for one moment. I just have an issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session. I don't know the reason yet, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having consulted my colleagues, Mr. Kehoe, I can speak on behalf of the Chamber that the Chamber is assisted by an approach in which you first establish the basis for opinions expressed by the witness at any time. We still do not know for sure whether apart from the army, whether that was what the gist of what his opinions was at the time, because we had some difficulties in establishing that. And then only after that, to compare that with others, whether in books, whether anywhere else, that is the appropriate way to elicit evidence from the witness which does assist the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Dr. Dodig, let me talk to you about your comment about The Hague Tribunal being a political Tribunal, or if you said that, or were of that belief back in 2001. Now, turning our attention to the Office of the Prosecution, were you of the belief during that period of time that you concluded or had the opinion that the Office of the Prosecutor of The Hague Tribunal was a political body?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, precisely the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what was the basis of that opinion, Dr. Dodig?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for that opinion was my perception from what I had been reading and hearing over the year; namely, that the Office of the Prosecutor is the predominant institution in this Tribunal, and that all that we hear from the Tribunal, as a three-pronged institution, is what the Office of the Prosecutor puts out. Conditions were always placed before Croatia, emanating from the Office of the Prosecutor, so the OTP had always been perceived as an institution within The Hague Tribunal who has a precise game plan and a clear objective, that objective being not to find individuals guilty of war crimes but individuals who symbolised the Croatian defence war, in terms of military and other leadership, people who I am deeply convinced play their role in that war very honourably. And, of course, I'm aware that there were individuals in the category of psychopaths that I mentioned who did do ugly, ugly things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand your conclusions, sir, and in the interests of time, you noted for us that you don't recall exactly what Ms. Hartmann had to say in her book --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's first try to explore that in as much detail. I do understand you answer to be that you said that for two reasons you considered the Office of the Prosecutor to be the predominant political element in the work of this Tribunal. The first being that always they were in the foreground; that's one. And, second, because they did not -- they were not after the guilty ones but they just wanted to attack the symbols who had honestly behaved. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now were there -- were there any other reasons, apart from the ones you mentioned, that contributed to you forming an opinion about the Tribunal or the Office of the Prosecutor as being political organs or bodies? Was there any other thing that comes to your mind what was at the basis of your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the basis of my -- my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was there were no other important elements at the basis of this opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing I -- in particular that I can think of, in this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, Judge Orie asked you about the two reasons for your position, and in line 18, Judge Orie said you considered for the two -- excuse me. You considered -- for two reasons you considered the Office of the Prosecutor to be a predominant political element in the work of this Tribunal, to which you responded yes. Were you aware that Florence Hartmann gave the same opinion as the opinion that you just articulated, concerning the Office of the Prosecutor being the predominant political element in the work of the Tribunal? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let me talk to you, go back, if we may, concerning Ms. Hartmann, her book, her discussions on media tours in Croatia, and what was printed in the press in Croatia, and you noted for us that you didn't recall exactly what you had read, so let me go to these excerpts from Ms. Hartmann's book, again, if I may, which is 65 ter 1D2986, and if we can view that via Sanction, and we are only going to look at three short excerpts on page 44, 47, 48 which have been translated into English. And if I may, at page 44, at the top, it notes: "Lawyers, military analysts and policemen from every country of the Commonwealth followed them and rushed to The Hague. France is falling behind. While the Prosecution and the procedure fall under Anglo-Saxon hands, Paris does not wish to participate in this effort. However, without a budget, the ICTY depends on contributions." It talks about a piece in France. Let me go down to the next paragraph, starting, "These differences ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, could you gave us the time-frame, because it says a year later, but I've got no idea in what year we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I will have Mr. Misetic, if he can, check the Croatian translation because the book itself, my understanding is that it has only been drafted in -- or written in -- published, excuse me, in French and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I just -- the part where it says "followed them," I'm just curious as to who "them" is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From Mr. Misetic's review of this, it appears that she is referring to the late 1990s, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Late 1990s. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Next paragraph: "These difference in the attitude between the French and the Anglo-Saxons were evident from the very start and they are not coincidental. All the realists in the Tribunal see ... the extenuation of the political -- of the political authority, its judicial branch. As soon as the effects of the announcement started to become obvious, everyone was in agreement that the goal was already accomplished. The ICTY was a means of justification for the politicians and as a vent for their [sic] emotions caused by the atrocities committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "Immediately afterward [sic] it was abandoned with no means to sustain itself with no budget. Against all expectations, a handful of sufficiently idealistic masters were going to pull it away from its fate of a worn-out alibi tossed in the waste basket. They knocked on every door and finally found funds to open their first investigations. "This unexpected awakening brought the great powers in an awkward position. They gave promises which they had no intention of keeping. They created obligations for themselves which they didn't perceive as binding. Now they will have to make a deal because the work of the Tribunal will undoubtedly have political implications. However, the great powers are still not responding as fast and with the same armament before this creature is slipping from their hands and the creature they are afraid."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They're talking about the Prosecution in this next paragraph, on page 42: "Some barely know where the Balkans even are [sic]. They are hounding the Prosecution, the moving force of the Tribunal, whose Judges have been subdued to the position of arbitraries between the Defence and Prosecution [sic]. Military analysts, lawyers, and intelligence officers easily blend in the crowed continuing to occupy humble yet strategic positions and serving more to their own governments than the ICTY." The last section, talking about Carla Del Ponte: "But at no time has she herself stated at the end of the [sic] mandate could she have imagined that the work of the international Prosecutor was so much different than the work of a state attorney, that [sic] there were so many pressures and attempts of political influence. Faced with the possibility of disobedience by the Prosecutors, the Anglo-Saxons could not content themselves with the mere sharing of advice which was so rarely followed. This why they simultaneously developed far more devious and dangerous strategics which the masters will not always able to detect in time." 24 Now, sir, Dr. Dodig, does that -- those excerpts refresh your recollection in any fashion concerning the position of the former spokesperson of the Office of the Prosecutor according -- discussing the political nature of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: GORAN DODIG [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. My memory is not refreshed. These were -- this was the way I saw it much before I read it. Based on things I may not be able to remember now and synthesising them all afterward, I appreciate the efforts and honour this Court, and I believe the Tribunal will do what it is supposed to do. And I will be only too glad if I come to the conclusion eventually that I was wrong and that this Tribunal is not political, and you may rest assured that I will certainly do so, and if -- if that happens, and I will explain to the people where I live that I was wrong about saying that this is a political body. We'll see whether that will happen or not, but after all this, I feel bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one last question for you. In your statement, you said that -- in paragraph 6: "Along the road which I took to Knin, there were only a few torched houses." This morning, page 17, lines 21, 22, you said that you could not see whether it was hay, or grass, or houses that produced smoke. Could you explain the difference in your perception when you gave this statement and when you gave your testimony this morning, where you said you couldn't see whether it was hay, or grass, or houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, I couldn't see -- or couldn't tell from a distance, and here where I say that I saw only a few houses on the road from Drnis to Knin, which is a distance of about 30 kilometres, no burnt house I saw there had been burned recently. So it was impossible for me to tell from travelling down that road, whether those houses were actually torched in Operation Storm or at some other time. So the houses may have been 200 or 300 metres away from the road. So it was really hard for me to tell whether that house or those houses had been burned recently or -- and whether or not they were burned in a military operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Any further questions triggered by the questions put to the witness by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, Mr. Dodig, this concludes your evidence in this Court. I would like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that you were put to you, questions by the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- parties and questions put to you by the Bench. I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as next week, Thursday, the 15th, is concerned, everyone is still working. If we would sit that whole day, then it should be expected that part of the day that the Chamber could sit only under Rule 15 bis, at least some part of the afternoon. Of course, the Chamber will have to consider, in view of the evidence we anticipate to receive, whether that would be in the interests of justice to proceed in the absence of one of the Judges, and, further, all the staffing issues have not yet been resolved. Everyone's working hard. We hope to know as soon as possible, whether it will be that Thursday. We'll then also consider what consequences this would have and the Cermak Defence is also invited consider what consequences that would have for the Wednesday, the 14th. Because I think, up till this moment, the two video-conference links were anticipated to take place on the 14th and the 15th. 14th is impossible. If we would sit more than half a day's session on the 15th, we have to consider what consequences that would have for the sessions on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can assist Your Honour with that, because we have the schedule for that week. We had the witness Mr. Cetina in the line for the first two days of that week, and then the -- one of the witnesses who had to go to hospital and would be free and available on the Wednesday, the 14th, so we cover those three days. It's really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be then be the witness who couldn't testify this week on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that would then be on -- that witness would be scheduled on Wednesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Wednesday, travelling Tuesday, arriving Wednesday. What it's coming down to now is this spare -- it's not a spare day. It's a day that's available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you are aware that if we would not conclude the testimony of that witness on Wednesday and if we are preparing for a videolink on Thursday, that irrespective of whether that witness would have concluded its testimony, that we would have to start with the videolink because that -- videolink prepared always takes precedence over any other witness waiting, because the technical facilities are not there forever. We should use them once they are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. He is not a big witness, looking at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But perhaps it would also be good also to discuss this briefly with the other parties and perhaps with the Prosecution to see whether that testimony of that witness could be concluded on that Wednesday so as to avoid that he has to stay over until Friday. Then we'll adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 8th of October, 9.00, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
